reference.source: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery / NICE-SIGN venous guidance
clinicalPearls: Venous leg ulcers are the commonest type of chronic leg ulcer and result from chronic venous insufficiency with sustained ambulatory venous hypertension
They characteristically lie in the gaiter area of the lower leg, most often over or just proximal to the medial malleolus
Ulcers are usually shallow with irregular sloping edges and a granulating, exudative base, and are typically only moderately painful

The surrounding skin shows chronic venous changes such as haemosiderin pigmentation, varicose eczema, lipodermatosclerosis, atrophie blanche and oedema, sometimes producing an inverted champagne-bottle contour
Arterial disease must be excluded before compression, as the ankle-brachial index determines whether compression, the mainstay of treatment, can be applied safely
Graduated compression with multilayer bandaging or hosiery substantially improves healing, and endovenous or surgical treatment of superficial reflux reduces recurrence
A chronic or atypical non-healing ulcer warrants biopsy to exclude malignant transformation such as a Marjolin ulcer or another diagnosis
Recurrence is common, so long-term compression hosiery, leg elevation, calf-muscle exercise and correction of underlying reflux are central to prevention
reference.pathophysiology: Venous valvular incompetence in the superficial, perforator or deep systems, venous outflow obstruction, or failure of the calf-muscle pump raises the ambulatory venous pressure transmitted to the lower leg. Persistent venous hypertension causes capillary distension and leakage of fibrinogen and macromolecules, forming pericapillary fibrin cuffs, and promotes leucocyte trapping with release of inflammatory mediators and proteases. The resulting chronic inflammation, dermal fibrosis and impaired tissue oxygenation render the gaiter skin fragile, so that minor trauma to this compromised tissue ulcerates and heals poorly.
additionalDifferentials: Marjolin ulcer (squamous cell carcinoma in a chronic ulcer)
additionalInvestigations: Ankle-brachial index to exclude arterial disease and enable safe compression
Venous duplex ultrasound to map sites of reflux and obstruction
Wound swab or tissue culture where clinical infection is present
Biopsy of atypical or non-healing ulcers to exclude malignancy
Assessment for diabetes and anaemia that may impair healing
Patch testing where contact allergy to dressings or topical agents is suspected
redFlags: Features suggesting malignant transformation, such as rolled or everted edges, exuberant granulation or failure to heal despite adequate treatment
Signs of spreading infection or cellulitis, or systemic sepsis
A sudden increase in pain, which may indicate coexisting arterial disease, infection or malignancy
Rapid deterioration or enlargement of the ulcer
reference.prognosis: Many venous ulcers heal with adequate compression and treatment of underlying reflux, although healing can be slow; recurrence is frequent unless compression is maintained and the underlying venous disease is corrected.
pitfalls: Starting compression without checking the ankle-brachial index and excluding arterial disease
Attributing every leg ulcer to venous disease without reassessment
Failing to biopsy a chronic non-healing ulcer
Applying inadequate compression so the ulcer fails to heal
Neglecting varicose eczema and skin care, or leaving underlying superficial reflux untreated so the ulcer recurs
references: NICE and SIGN guidance on the management of venous leg ulcers
Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
European guidelines on chronic venous disease
management: Apply graduated multilayer compression bandaging or hosiery as the mainstay of healing, only after excluding significant arterial disease with the ankle-brachial index
Provide wound care with cleansing, debridement of slough, simple non-adherent dressings and exudate management
Treat underlying superficial venous reflux with endovenous ablation to accelerate healing and reduce recurrence
Manage venous eczema of the surrounding skin with emollients and topical corticosteroids, reserving systemic antibiotics for clinical infection rather than colonisation
Encourage leg elevation, exercise and calf-muscle pump activity, and correct contributors to poor healing such as anaemia, diabetes and poor nutrition
Maintain long-term compression hosiery once healed to prevent recurrence
Biopsy atypical or non-healing ulcers to exclude malignancy and refer to tissue viability and vascular services
